transcript.text: While reconciling the late-produced onboarding export against our user-agreement database, I confirmed that exactly 312 of the 480 putative class members have executed agreements containing an arbitration provision. The remaining 168 do not have arbitration provisions in their agreements. This means we can only compel arbitration for roughly 65% of the putative class, and the other 168 would remain in litigation regardless. I have not yet incorporated this reconciliation into the formal arbitration analysis, but it clearly affects our leverage and the scope of any arbitration strategy. I wanted to surface this now so it can inform Marisol's response strategy and so we can consider how it interacts with whatever Talia has from the client's business review.

transcript.text: Here's the client update I mentioned. During this week's business review, the client confirmed that they will keep the automated referral feature available, but will withdraw all referral-related marketing claims and complete that withdrawal within exactly 60 days, without admitting wrongdoing. The client has not yet put this position into the litigation strategy memo, so I want to make sure it's on the table here as Marisol develops the response strategy. Evan, this is particularly relevant to your findings — the 168 users without arbitration provisions would still be in litigation, and the marketing claim withdrawal could directly address the merits of their claims even where we can't compel arbitration.

transcript.text:
Thank you both. This is exactly why we review discovery status and client business constraints together before I issue the binding response strategy. Let me synthesize what we now have on the table.

Evan, your reconciliation is critical. We can only compel arbitration for 312 of the 480 putative class members — the remaining 168 stay in court regardless. That fundamentally changes our arbitration posture. A partial arbitration motion still leaves us exposed on the merits for over a third of the class, and it risks bifurcating proceedings in a way that could be inefficient and create inconsistent narratives.

Talia, the client's position actually complements Evan's findings well. If the client is willing to withdraw all referral-related marketing claims within 60 days without admitting wrongdoing, that directly addresses the merits of the misleading-marketing allegation — and it covers the 168 users we cannot arbitrate. It also aligns with the limited injunction approach we've already proposed.

So here's my preliminary thinking before I formalize the strategy: We pursue arbitration for the 312 users who have arbitration provisions, while simultaneously leveraging the marketing-claims withdrawal as the merits response for the remaining 168. The referral feature stays operational, but the marketing claims come down within the 60-day window. No admission of wrongdoing. This gives us a coherent two-track strategy — arbitration where we can, and substantive relief where we can't.

Let me take one more moment to consider the interaction between these items before I issue the formal response strategy. Are there any other discovery or business items I should factor in before I finalize?
